lessons.title: Hello, students! (Greetings)
match: Different expressions of greetings
objectives: Greet people and answer greetings.
Use the verb to be (am, is, are) in short greetings.
lessons.intro: I enter the class and say: “Hello, students! How are you?” I wait for their answers, then I ask: “What do we say when we meet someone?”
lessons.summary: In the dialogue, the teacher Mohamed meets his first-year class: “Hello, students, how are you?” – “Hello.” – “My name is Mohamed. What is your name?” To greet, we say: hi, hello, good morning. To answer “How are you?” we say: I am fine / fine, thank you / thanks. The verb to be in the simple present: I am (I’m); he, she, it is (he’s, she’s, it’s); we, you, they are (we’re, you’re, they’re).
points: Greetings: hi, hello, how are you?
Answers: I am fine, fine, thank you, thanks.
I am = I’m; he/she/it is; we/you/they are.
Adjectives: good, fine, okay.

lines: Mohamed: Hello, students, how are you?
Students: Hello. Are you a teacher?
Mohamed: Yes, I am. My name is Mohamed. What is your name?
Aly: My name is Aly.
Aly: Oh, the bell is ringing. I’m going home, goodbye! — Demba: Bye-bye!
Greetings: hi / hello / how are you? — I am fine / fine, thank you / thanks.
Adjectives: good, fine, okay.
Vocabulary: good, goodbye, morning, hello, how are you, fine, bye-bye.

lessons.title: Goodbye, bye-bye! (Leave taking)
match: Leave taking expressions
objectives: Greet according to the time of the day.
Take leave politely.
lessons.intro: I ask: “What do you say to your friends when you leave school at the end of the day?”
lessons.summary: We greet according to the time: good morning, good afternoon, good evening. When we meet someone for the first time we say: “Nice to meet you” – “Nice to meet you, too”. To take leave we say: goodbye, bye-bye, see you. We use the subject pronouns I, you, he, she, it, the wh- words how, what, where, and the verb to be: am, is, are.
points: Good + morning / afternoon / evening.
Nice to meet you. – Nice to meet you, too.
Leave taking: goodbye, bye-bye, see you.
Wh- words: how, what, where.

application.q: What do you say at 8 a.m.? At 4 p.m.? When you leave?
application.a: Good morning. Good afternoon. Goodbye / Bye-bye.

lines: Saleh: Hi, good morning. Are you a new student? What is your name?
Zeineb: Yes, I’m a new student coming from Zouerate. My name is Zeineb.
John: Good afternoon. My name is John. — Moussa: My name is Moussa. It’s a pleasure to meet you.
Abdalla: Nice to meet you, Diagana. — Diagana: Where are you from? — Abdalla: I’m from Turkey!
Good morning — Good afternoon — Good evening.
How are you? — I’m fine / I’m okay.
Nice to meet you. — Nice to meet you, too.
Bye — Goodbye.
Good + morning / afternoon / evening.
Subject pronouns: I, you, he, she, it.
“Wh” words: how, what, where.
To be in the simple present: am, is, are.

lessons.title: Counting (1–50)
match: Counting (1-50)
objectives: Count from 0 to 50.
Say and understand phone numbers.
lessons.intro: I write some numbers on the board (7, 13, 20, 45) and ask: “Who can read these numbers in English?”
lessons.summary: The book gives the numbers from zero to fifty: one, two, three… ten; eleven, twelve, thirteen… nineteen; twenty, twenty-one… thirty, forty, fifty. We use numbers to say our age (I am 13 years old) and our phone numbers: “His number is two, six, eight, five…”.
points: 0–10: zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
11–19: eleven, twelve, thirteen … nineteen.
Tens: twenty, thirty, forty, fifty.
Compound numbers: twenty-one, thirty-five, forty-eight…
How old are you? – I am 13 years old.

lines: How old are you? — I am twelve. / I am 15 years old.
Djeinaba: I’m sixteen. And you? — Fatma: I am fourteen.

lessons.title: Talking about oneself
match: Introducing oneself, responding to introductions and asking for and giving personal information
objectives: Introduce oneself and respond to introductions.
Ask for and give personal information: name, origin, residence, age.
Introduce others.
lessons.intro: I introduce myself: “Hello! My name is … I am from … I live in …”. Then I ask a student: “And you? What is your name?”
lessons.summary: To talk about ourselves we say: My name is Sara. I am from Kaedi. I live in Atar. Our nationality is Mauritanian. To ask: What is your name? Where are you from? Where do you live? How old are you? When we meet someone: “Glad to meet you” – “Glad to meet you, too.” To introduce others: “Let me introduce you to Mody, my brother.” / “This is my classmate, Behah.”
points: My name is … / I am from … / I live in …
What is your name? Where are you from? Where do you live?
Glad / Nice to meet you. – Glad to meet you, too.
Introducing others: Let me introduce you to … / This is …
Possessive adjective: your (What is your name?).

application.q: Complete: My ___ is Savia. I ___ from Mauritania and I ___ in Boutilimit.
application.a: My name is Savia. I am from Mauritania and I live in Boutilimit.

lines: Hello. I am a student in this class. My name is Sara. What’s your name?
Hi. My name is Khadija. I live in Atar.
Hello. My name is Ramata. I am from Kaedi.
Our nationality is Mauritanian.
To be: I am. To have: I have.
Short forms: I’m, you’re, he’s, she’s, we’re ; I’ve, you’ve, we’ve, they’ve ; name’s.
Personal pronoun: I. Possessive adjectives: my, your.
Use capital letters for proper names and the beginning of a sentence.
Nice to meet you, Ahmed. — Nice to meet you, too.
Glad to meet you. — Glad to meet you, too.
Good night! See you tomorrow!
Let me introduce you to Mody, my brother. — I’d like you to meet my best friend Fatima.
Pleased to meet you. — It’s a pleasure to meet you, too.
Nationalities: He is Mauritanian. She is Japanese.

lessons.title: The alphabet
match: The alphabet: sound and script
objectives: Say and write the letters of the alphabet (capital and small).
Spell names.
lessons.intro: I ask: “How do you spell your name?” and I spell my own name letter by letter on the board.
lessons.summary: The English alphabet has 26 letters. Each letter has a capital form (A, B, C…) and a small form (a, b, c…). We use the alphabet to spell names: “How do you spell his last name?” – “A-b-d-e-r-r-a-h-m-a-n-e.”
points: 26 letters: A to Z.
Capital letters: A B C D …
Small letters: a b c d …
How do you spell it, please?

application.q: Spell your first name and your town.

N O P Q R S T U V W X Y Z

n o p q r s t u v w x y z
“C-o-u-m-b-a D-i-e-n-g” — you write: Coumba Dieng.
How do you spell your last name, please? — It’s M-U-L-L-E-R.

lessons.title: Demonstratives (identifying things)
match: Demonstratives
objectives: Identify things with this, that, these, those.
Ask if someone has an object.
lessons.intro: I hold a pen and say: “This is a pen.” Then I point to the door: “That is a door.” I ask: “What is this?”
lessons.summary: In the market, Mahmoud asks the shopkeeper: “Can I have that jacket, please?” – “Which one?” – “The blue one.” This and that are used for singular; these and those for plural. This / these: for close things; that / those: for far things. To ask if someone has an object: Do you have a …? Does he / she have a …?
points: This / That + singular: This is a fan.
These / Those + plural: These are pens.
This, these: close. That, those: far.
Do you have a …? Does he have a …?

application.q: Fill in with is / are: This ___ a fan. These ___ not pens. That ___ a lighter.
application.a: This is a fan. These are not pens. That is a lighter.

lines: Mahmoud: Can I have that jacket, please? — Shopkeeper: Which one? — Mahmoud: The blue one.
Mahmoud: How much is it? — Shopkeeper: It’s 800 MRU.
Mahmoud: And how much are those shoes? — Shopkeeper: They’re 300 MRU.
What is this? — This is a watch. / It’s a watch.
What are those? — Those are shoes.
Rooms: hall, living room, dining room, bathroom, bedroom, kitchen.
Do you have a refrigerator? — Does she have a washing machine?

lessons.title: Listen to me! (Instructions)
match: Responding and giving classroom positive and negative commands/instructions
objectives: Give and respond to positive and negative instructions in the classroom.
lessons.intro: I say: “Stand up! … Sit down! … Open your books!” and the students do the actions. Then I ask: “What did I do?”
lessons.summary: In the dialogue, the teacher reviews the classroom rules: “Look at me! Listen very carefully! Be on time! Don’t sit on the tables!” A positive instruction uses the simple form of the verb: Listen to me! A negative instruction uses Don’t + the simple form of the verb: Don’t sit on the table!
points: Positive instruction: verb (simple form): Listen! Open your book!
Negative instruction: Don’t + verb: Don’t talk!
Classroom rules: Be on time! Clean the board! Respect the elders!

lines: Look at me! Listen to me! Be on time! Clean the board!
Write the date! Write with a blue pen! Behave yourselves!
Don’t sit on the tables!
Don’t throw pieces of paper on the floor!
Don’t spit on the wall!
Don’t write with a red pen or a pencil!
Positive instruction: simple form of the verb — Listen to me!
Negative instruction: Don’t + simple form of the verb — Don’t sit on the table!
Vocabulary: stand up, sit down, come in, go out, knock on the door, obey your parents, respect the elders.

lessons.title: What time is it?
match: Telling and asking for the time
objectives: Ask for and tell the time.
Say the time of day (a.m. / p.m.).
lessons.intro: I draw a clock on the board showing 8:00 and ask: “What time is it?”
lessons.summary: To ask the time: What time is it? What’s the time? Do you have the time, please? To answer: It is eleven o’clock. It is seven-thirty / half past seven. It is twenty past six. We say a.m. (in the morning) and p.m. (in the afternoon, in the evening, at night). Examples: I wake up at seven-thirty in the morning. School ends at noon.
points: What time is it? / What’s the time?
It is … o’clock.
Half past, … past, … to.
a.m. = morning; p.m. = afternoon / evening / night.
noon (12:00 p.m.), midnight (12:00 a.m.).

application.q: Write the time: 7:30 a.m. and 4:00 p.m.
application.a: It is seven-thirty (half past seven) in the morning. It is four o’clock in the afternoon.

table: It is six-twenty / twenty past six.
It is seven-thirty p.m. / half past seven.
It is eight thirty-five / twenty-five to nine.
It is nine forty-five / a quarter to ten.

lines: a.m.: from midnight to midday ; p.m.: from midday to midnight.
Midday is 12:00 ; midnight is 00:00.
From … to …: I go to school from eight in the morning to one in the afternoon.
What time is it? — What’s the time? — Do you have time, please?
Sorry, could you tell me the time, please?
What time does this class begin? — It begins at 10:00 a.m.

lessons.title: Today is Monday (Days of the week)
match: The seven days of the week
objectives: Name the seven days of the week in order.
lessons.intro: I ask: “What day is it today?” and I write the answer on the board.
lessons.summary: There are seven days in a week: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Monday is the first day of the week, Tuesday is the second … Sunday is the seventh day. Days always start with a capital letter.
points: Seven days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
Monday is the first day of the week.
Days start with a capital letter.

application.q: Complete: ___ is the fifth day of the week. Monday is the ___ day of the week.
application.a: Friday is the fifth day. Monday is the first day.

lines: There are seven days in a week.
Monday is the first day of the week ; Sunday is the seventh day.
Vocabulary: day, week, today, before, after, first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh.

lessons.title: Show me today’s date (Months and date)
match: The twelve months of the year
Giving, asking for and writing the date
objectives: Name the twelve months of the year.
Ask for, give and write the date.
lessons.intro: I write today’s date on the board and ask: “What is the date today?”
lessons.summary: There are twelve months in a year: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November and December. January is the first month, December is the twelfth. To ask the date: What is the date today? To answer: Today is Monday, the fourth of November. We write: Monday, November 4th.
points: Twelve months: January … December.
January is the first month; December is the twelfth.
What is the date today?
Today is … the … of …
Months start with a capital letter.

application.q: Complete: ___ is the eighth month of the year. Write today’s date.
application.a: August is the eighth month. Example: Today is Wednesday, November 4th.

lines: There are twelve months in a year.
January is the first month of the year ; December is the twelfth month.
Vocabulary: independence, day, month, year.

lessons.title: Talking about others (family and friends)
match: Asking for and giving one's family members' and friends' personal information
objectives: Ask for and give information about family members and friends.
Use he / she, his / her and the simple present (live, have).
lessons.intro: I show a photo of a family and ask: “Who is this man? What is his name? Where does he live?”
lessons.summary: Mohamed asks Abdoul about his new friend Ahmed: “What’s his name? Where is he from?” Omar introduces his family in a WhatsApp message: “This man is my father, Sow, he is a policeman.” We use he / she, his / her, contractions (he’s, she’s, his name’s) and nationalities (Mauritanian, Canadian…). Simple present: I live – he lives; I don’t live – he doesn’t live; I have – he has.
points: Personal pronouns: he, she. Possessive adjectives: his, her.
Contractions: he is → he’s, her name is → her name’s.
Nationalities: Mauritania → Mauritanian.
He / she lives, has; he / she doesn’t live, doesn’t have.

application.q: Write three sentences about a member of your family.
application.a: Example: My brother’s name is Ali. He is twelve years old. He lives in Kiffa.

lines: Abdoul: He is a first year student. He is from Tidjikja, but now he lives in Ksar with his aunt.
His father is a teacher, and his mother is a nurse. He has two brothers and one sister.

table: No, he doesn’t. He lives in Ksar.

lines: Personal pronouns: he, she ; possessive adjectives: his, her.
Contractions: he is → he’s ; she is → she’s ; where is → where’s ; his name is → his name’s.
Mauritania → Mauritanian ; Mali → Malian ; Tunisia → Tunisian ; Canada → Canadian.
England → English ; France → French ; the United States → American.

lessons.title: At a party (Identifying people)
match: Demonstratives and relative pronouns
objectives: Identify people using demonstratives and descriptions (in + clothing, with + accessories).
lessons.intro: I point to a student and ask: “Who is that boy in the blue shirt?”
lessons.summary: At Ahmed’s party, Yacoub asks: “Who is that boy in a blue shirt?” – “He is my brother, Baba.” “And who are those boys?” We identify people with: in + clothing (the boy in a grey jacket is my nephew) and with + body parts / accessories (the man with a mask is a doctor).
points: Who is that boy …? Who are those girls …?
in + clothing: the girl in a red dress.
with + accessories / body parts: the man with a cap.
that / those for people who are far.

application.q: Fill in with in / with: The man ___ a black suit is the headmaster. The boy ___ a cap is Samba.
application.a: The man in a black suit … The boy with a cap …

lines: Yacoub: Ahmed, who is that boy in a blue shirt? — Ahmed: He is my brother, Baba.
Yacoub: What about the girl wearing a veil? — Ahmed: She’s my sister, Khadija.
Yacoub: And who are those boys? — Ahmed: They are my classmates, Abdou and Adama.
in + clothing: The boy in a grey jacket is my nephew.
with + body parts / accessories: The man with a mask is a doctor.
Vocabulary: party, to invite, who, in, with, cap, veil, pants, gloves, turban, jeans.

lessons.title: Where are these balls? (Locating)
match: Ask about and say where people and things are located
objectives: Ask about and say where people and things are.
lessons.intro: I put a pen on the table, then under the table, and ask: “Where is the pen?”
lessons.summary: Sidi, Fatimetou and Demba are on the bus. Salem is under the car. Ali is behind the car. Lalla is in front of the car. Fatimetou is between Demba and Sidi. To ask: Where is …? Where are …? Prepositions of location: in, on, at, under, behind, in front of, between, above, below, across.
points: Where is …? / Where are …?
Prepositions: in, on, at, under, behind, in front of, between, above, below.
Example: The teacher is in front of the students.

application.q: Complete: The teacher stands ___ the students. Fatimetou is ___ Demba and Sidi.

lines: Salem is under the car. Samba and Omar are in the car.
Ali is behind the car. Lalla is in front of the car.
Fatimetou is between Demba and Sidi.
Where is the teacher? — He is in front of the students.
Where are Sidi and Khady? — They are behind Zeinebou.
Where is the teacher’s bag? — It’s on the desk.
Prepositions of location: in, on, at, under, behind, in front of, between, next to, above, below, across.

lessons.title: Describing things
match: Describing things giving their sizes, shapes, quality, colors, origin…
objectives: Describe things: size, shape, colour, quality.
Use possessive pronouns.
lessons.intro: I show a book and ask: “What colour is it? Is it big or small? Is it heavy?”
lessons.summary: To describe things we use adjectives: large, small, hot, cold, black, red, square, rectangular, oval, good, bad… Adjectives never take “s”. Questions: What’s it like? – It’s … What colour is …? What’s the colour of …? Possessive pronouns: mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs.
points: Adjectives of size, shape, colour, quality.
Adjectives never take “s”: two red books.
What’s it like? What colour is it?
Possessive pronouns: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.

application.q: Describe your schoolbag with two adjectives.
application.a: Example: My schoolbag is big and blue.

lines: Her schoolbag is heavy. His shoes are dirty. Our classroom is large.
My shirt is new. Your ruler is triangular. Their class is noisy.

lines: Adjectives (never take “s”): large, small, hot, cold, black, red, square, rectangular, oval, good, bad.
Possessive pronouns: mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs.
What’s it like? — It’s … ; What are they like? — They are …
What’s the color of …? — What color is …?

lessons.title: Describing people
match: Describing people giving their height, weight, age, personal character, physical traits, state, clothing, body parts
objectives: Describe people: height, age, physical traits, clothing.
lessons.intro: I describe a student without saying his name: “He is tall, he has short hair, he is wearing a white shirt.” Who is it?
lessons.summary: Ahmed is wearing a red shirt. Khady is ten years old; she has black hair; she is a short girl. To describe people we use: He / she is … (tall, short, fat, thin, young, old). He / she has got … (long hair, a beard). He / she wears … To ask: What does he / she look like?
points: He / she is + adjective: tall, short, thin, young.
He / she has got + noun: long hair, a beard.
He / she wears / is wearing + clothes.
What does he / she look like?

application.q: Describe a classmate in two sentences.
application.a: Example: Salma is tall and thin. She has long hair.

lines: Ahmed is wearing a red shirt. Ahmed is twelve years old.
My sister Khady is ten years old. She has black hair. She is a short girl.
What does she look like? — She is tall with a broad nose.
What color is her hair? — It is black. What color are her eyes? — They are brown.
What does she usually wear? — She usually wears a blue veil.
Adjectives never take “s”.
He/she has got … ; He/she wears … ; He/she is …
Has he/she got …? Is he/she …? What does he/she look like?
a toddler: around 1–3 years old ; a teenager: between 13 and 19.
lean: with very little fat ; wavy hair: between straight and curly.
a snub nose: a nose which goes up at the end ; a broad nose ≠ a narrow nose.

lessons.title: They can do (Ability)
match: Expressing what one can or can't do
objectives: Express ability and inability with can / can’t.
lessons.intro: I ask: “Can you swim? Can you speak English?” and students answer yes or no.
lessons.summary: Ability: Aminetou can listen to music. Fatma can read. Inability: Ali can’t see. Ousmane can’t speak. To ask a question, we invert the subject and can: Can you drive? Short answers: Yes, I can / No, I can’t.
points: Ability: subject + can + verb.
Inability: subject + can’t (cannot) + verb.
Question: Can + subject + verb?
Short answers: Yes, I can. / No, I can’t.

application.q: Answer: Can you speak Hassaniya? Can you fly with your arms?
application.a: Yes, I can. / No, I can’t.

lines: Aminetou can listen to music. Fatma can read.
Ali can’t see. Ousmane can’t speak. Khadi can’t play football.
To form a question, invert the subject and “can”: Can you drive? Can he drive?
Short answers: Yes, I can. / No, I can’t. — Yes, she can. / No, she can’t.
Vocabulary: blind, deaf, dumb, crippled, jump, run, ride, of course.

lessons.title: Daily routine (Habitual actions)
match: Talking about routines and frequency of actions
objectives: Talk about habitual actions with the simple present.
Use frequency adverbs.
lessons.intro: I ask: “What time do you wake up? What do you do before school?”
lessons.summary: “On a typical day, I wake up at six o’clock, I do my ablutions and pray, I eat my breakfast…” The simple present is used for habitual actions: I / you / we / they write; he / she / it writes. Negative: I don’t write; he doesn’t write. Frequency adverbs: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never.
points: Simple present for routines.
He / she / it + verb + s: he writes.
Negative: don’t / doesn’t + verb.
Frequency adverbs: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never.

application.q: Write three sentences about your morning routine.
application.a: Example: I always wake up at six. I usually eat breakfast. I never come late.

lines: I wake up at six o’clock in the morning ; I do my ablutions and pray.
I eat my breakfast and brush my teeth, then I go to school and stay there until two o’clock.
In the evening, I study my lessons, eat dinner with my family and watch television. Then I go to bed.

board.h: I can remember: the simple present
lines: The present tense is used to talk about habitual actions.
table: Do you drink tea? — Yes, I do.
Does he bring his phone? — No, he doesn’t.

lines: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never.
I always drink milk in the morning. He sometimes plays football. I rarely go to the sea.

lessons.title: Different tasks (Ongoing actions)
match: Asking and answering questions about what one is presently doing
objectives: Describe ongoing actions with the present continuous.
lessons.intro: I start writing on the board and ask: “What am I doing now?”
lessons.summary: He is watching television. She is cooking. We are studying English. The present continuous describes an ongoing action: be (am, is, are) + verb + ing. Questions: What are you doing? – I am making some tea. Spelling: take → taking, cut → cutting, begin → beginning.
points: Present continuous: am / is / are + verb-ing.
What are you doing? – I am …
Spelling: take → taking, cut → cutting.

application.q: Put the verb in the present continuous: Demba (pray). The teacher (write) a note.
application.a: Demba is praying. The teacher is writing a note.

lines: He is watching television. She is cooking. We are studying English.
What are you doing? — I am making some tea.
What are the children doing? — They are playing.
The present continuous describes an ongoing action.
Form: am / is / are + verb + ing — The teacher is explaining the lesson.
Spelling: take → taking ; cut → cutting ; begin → beginning.

lessons.title: Which game do you like? (Likes and dislikes)
match: Asking and answering questions about what one likes/dislikes
objectives: Ask and answer about likes and dislikes.
lessons.intro: I ask: “Do you like football? What is your favourite sport?”
lessons.summary: Sidi asks Ousmane about his hobbies: “Do you play football?” – “Yes, I do. I love playing football.” We say: I like + verb-ing / + noun (I like football, I like reading). I don’t like / I dislike / I hate + verb-ing. Questions: Do you like …? What is your favourite …?
points: I like / love + verb-ing or noun.
I don’t like / dislike / hate + verb-ing.
Do you like …? – Yes, I do. / No, I don’t.
What is your favourite …?

application.q: Talk about two things you like and one thing you dislike.
application.a: Example: I like reading and playing football. I don’t like hot weather.

lines: Sidi: Hey, Ousmane. Do you play football?
Ousmane: Yes, I do. I love playing football in the afternoon. What about you?
Sidi: I like football but my favorite sport is boxing.
Football is my favorite sport. Apples are my favorite fruit. Green is my favorite colour.
I like + verb-ing / + infinitive ;  I like + noun / pronoun.
Do you like + verb-ing?
I dislike + verb-ing.
